# Optional topic: Latent growth curves {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: @byrne2016, chapter 11, pp. 339–364 (about 90 minutes)

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd), waves file (`student_life_waves`)

App
: Latent growth curve sandbox

Task style
: Independent: plan and carry out the analysis yourself; the session reviews your plan

:::

## By the end of this week you can

- Specify intercept and slope factors with fixed loadings.
- Interpret growth-factor means, variances and their covariance.
- Test for non-linear change by freeing a loading.

## This week in brief

A latent growth curve model describes change over time with an intercept factor (starting level) and a slope factor (rate of change). Their means describe the average trajectory; their variances and covariance describe individual differences. Use this topic if your project has three or more measurement occasions.

## In the session

- Specifying the model with fixed loadings and a mean structure.
- Interpreting the growth parameters.
- Recoding time and freeing loadings for non-linear change, with the app.

## After the session

Read the core reading, and @curran2010 for twelve common questions about growth models.

## Your task this week

1. Fit a linear growth model to the four stress scores in the waves file (time codes 0, 1, 2, 3).
2. Free the loading for week 11. What value does it take, and what does that say about stress during the semester?
3. Add `year` as a predictor of the intercept and slope. Do first-year students' stress levels change differently?

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. What does the intercept represent under your time coding?
2. What does the freed week 11 loading tell you?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. The expected stress level at the occasion coded 0: week 2 of the semester.
2. If it is clearly above 3, stress rises faster towards the end of the semester (around assessments) than a straight line implies.

</details>
